questions.topic: Flow speed from a volume flow rate
questions.learningObjective: Compute flow speed from volume flow rate and pipe area
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, a stock pipe of area 0.02 m^2 carries 0.04 m^3/s of broth; find the flow speed in m/s.

options.text: The speed equals 2.0 m/s from flow rate divided by area
The speed equals 2.0 m/s when multiplying flow rate by area
The speed equals 0.8 m/s when dividing area by flow rate
The speed equals 0.0008 m/s by misplacing the decimal point

questions.explanation: Flow speed is volume flow rate over cross-sectional area, so 0.04/0.02=2.0 m/s. Multiplying gives an area-times-rate value with wrong units.
questions.hint: Divide volume flow rate by area.

questions.topic: Fraction of a body left under water
questions.learningObjective: Find the submerged fraction of a floating body
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet lists a wooden ladle of density 600 kg/m^3 floating in water; what fraction stays submerged?

options.text: Forty percent remains below because density is subtracted
Sixty percent of the ladle remains below the surface
One hundred percent sinks because wood absorbs water
Zero percent floats since wood is lighter than water

questions.explanation: Submerged fraction equals object density over fluid density, 600/1000=0.6. The complement is above water, not below.
questions.hint: Divide object density by water density.

questions.topic: Apparent weight in a lighter liquid
questions.learningObjective: Compute apparent mass of a block in oil
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, a 5.0 kg block hangs in oil of density 800 kg/m^3 with volume 0.002 m^3; find apparent mass in kg.
questions.explanation: Buoyant mass equals displaced fluid mass 800*0.002=1.6 kg, so apparent mass is 5.0-1.6=3.4 kg. Ignoring displacement keeps the full mass.
questions.hint: Subtract displaced fluid mass from true mass.

questions.topic: Tension needed to hold a block under water
questions.learningObjective: Find tension to hold a block fully submerged
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet holds a 0.01 m^3 wooden block under water; density 600 kg/m^3. Find tension in newtons.

options.text: Tension equals 0 N since wood floats freely
Tension equals 58.8 N as weight minus buoyancy
Tension equals 98.0 N using full water weight
Tension equals 39.2 N downward from buoyancy minus weight

questions.explanation: Buoyancy 98.0 N minus weight 58.8 N leaves 39.2 N downward tension. Weight alone is not the tension.

questions.topic: Mass flow rate in a pipe
questions.learningObjective: Compute mass flow rate from density and volume flow
questions.stem: In a chef's recipe costing sheet, water of density 1000 kg/m^3 flows at 0.03 m^3/s through a pipe; find mass flow rate in kg/s.

options.text: Mass flow rate equals 0.03 kg/s ignoring density
Mass flow rate equals 30 kg/s from density times volume flow
Mass flow rate equals 30000 kg/s by multiplying by 1000 twice
Mass flow rate equals 3 kg/s with a decimal slip

questions.explanation: Mass flow rate is density times volume flow rate, 1000*0.03=30 kg/s. Volume flow alone is not mass flow.
questions.hint: Multiply density by volume flow rate.

questions.topic: Driving frequency at resonance
questions.stem: A chef's recipe costing sheet vibrates a bowl at its natural frequency; what happens to amplitude?

options.text: Amplitude halves at the natural frequency
Amplitude stays zero at the natural frequency
Amplitude grows large at the natural frequency
Amplitude becomes constant regardless of drive

questions.explanation: Resonance occurs when drive frequency matches natural frequency, giving large amplitude. Off-resonance drives produce smaller response.

questions.topic: Force needed to submerge a floating block
questions.learningObjective: Compute downward force to submerge a floating block

stimulus.body: A costing sheet table lists block volume 0.005 m^3, block density 700 kg/m^3, and water density 1000 kg/m^3. It asks for the extra downward force to fully submerge the block.

questions.stem: Using the table values, find the extra downward force needed to fully submerge the block in newtons.

options.text: The force equals 0 N since block already floats
The force equals 34.3 N using block weight only
options.misconception: uses block weight instead of extra buoyancy

options.text: The force equals 49.0 N using full water weight
The force equals 14.7 N from extra displaced water

questions.explanation: Extra displaced volume when fully submerged is (1000-700)*0.005*9.8=14.7 N. This balances the added push.
questions.hint: Use density difference times volume times g.

questions.topic: Gauge pressure under two stacked liquids
questions.learningObjective: Compute gauge pressure under stacked liquids
questions.stem: Explain why gauge pressure at the bottom of two stacked liquids equals rho1 g h1 plus rho2 g h2.

answer.exemplar: Gauge pressure increases with depth in each liquid independently, so the total at the bottom is the sum of the pressure contributions rho1 g h1 and rho2 g h2 from each layer.

questions.explanation: Each layer adds hydrostatic pressure rho g h, and pressures add because the fluid is static. The wrong idea treats only the top layer.
questions.hint: Add pressure contributions from both layers.

questions.topic: Driving frequency at resonance
questions.stem: Explain why increasing damping lowers the resonance peak amplitude.

answer.exemplar: Damping removes energy each cycle, so less energy accumulates at resonance and the peak amplitude is lower and broader.

questions.explanation: Damping dissipates mechanical energy, reducing the maximum amplitude at resonance. Without damping the peak would be unbounded.

questions.topic: Force needed to submerge a floating block
questions.stem: Explain why a floating block needs extra downward force to be fully submerged.

answer.exemplar: At float equilibrium buoyancy equals weight; pushing it fully under displaces more water, so extra downward force must balance that additional buoyancy.

questions.explanation: Full submersion displaces more water than floating, increasing buoyancy. Extra downward force restores equilibrium.
questions.hint: Compare displaced volumes floating versus submerged.
